newsitem.title: JAPAN: Peru move lets Japan PM escape no-win situation.
newsitem.headline: Peru move lets Japan PM escape no-win situation.

text.p: The dramatic hostage rescue at the Japanese compound in Peru removed a major headache for Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who would have suffered if it had ended in failure, analysts said on Wednesday.

Hashimoto's limited role in the crisis was underscored by the fact he was not told by Lima in advance of the attack by 140 crack Peruvian soldiers, a development which detracted from Tokyo's obvious relief at the end of the ordeal.
Hashimoto mixed praise at President Alberto Fujimori's decisive strike with "regret" at not being informed.
"How can anyone criticise President Fujimori? It is not important whether we had prior knowledge of the move. The important thing is that the hostages were freed," he said.
Although the crisis united Japan's fractious political parties, the opposition read meaning into Lima's decision to act first and tell Tokyo later.

"That there was no prior notice shows how little confidence the international community has in Japan's crisis management," said Takeo Nishioka, general secretary of the main opposition New Frontier Party.
For Hashimoto, the 126-day hostage drama often appeared a no-win situation.

On the one hand, he felt strong domestic political pressure to show he was in charge after the previous Tokyo government came under criticism for inadequate responses to a devastating earthquake and terrorism on Tokyo subways in 1995.

The Japanese prime minister also had to demonstrate that his government was tougher on terrorism than it had been in the past, when Japan drew widespread criticism for agreeing to terrorists' demands in a series of 1970s hijackings.
On the other hand, Hashimoto faced a Japanese public whose deep-seated pacifism makes Tokyo leaders squeamish about even discussing security matters, let alone calling for military action.
The prime minister was thus forced to continuously insist on a peaceful, negotiated outcome while saying it would not give in to hostage-takers' demands.
That stance was logically inconsistent, caused occasional friction between Tokyo and Lima and may have led rebels to believe that, sooner or later, Japan would agree to a deal, security experts said.

Even Hashimoto's political gestures -- he personally delivered boxes of sweat buns to beleaguered officials monitoring the crisis -- were dismissed by experts as telegraphing the prime minister's helplessness to the hostage-takers in Lima.

Hashimoto alluded to the difficulty of coming to grips with a crisis half a world away after he learned that 71 hostages had been freed in a daring daytime raid by Peruvian commandos. The commandos killed 14 guerrillas and one Peruvian hostage in the assault, in which two soldiers also died.
"We were truly hoping for a peaceful solution, but that is a notion of someone who is far away at a place where there is a 14-hour time difference," Hashimoto said.
As the hostage crisis went from weeks to months, the issue was consistently cited as a reason for the steady erosion of Hashimoto's approval ratings in monthly media polls.

The standoff grew into a nagging distraction as Hashimoto grappled with other key policy issues, including a dispute with the southern island of Okinawa which threatened to undermine the Japan-U.S. security alliance.

Hashimoto last week pushed through parliament legislation to override Okinawan landowners' refusal to lease their land to the central government for use by the U.S. military, clearing the way for a meeting on Friday with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Washington.

Although the end of the hostage crisis removes one of the biggest challenges to Hashimoto's five-month old administration, it is not likely to benefit the prime minister politically, a political analyst said.
"Events on the international stage have virtually no impact on the world of Japanese politics," said pundit Minoru Morita.
